content:
Former US President Obama on Friday launched a fierce criticism against President Trump's decision to bar reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from accessing the White House.

Speaking in a conversation with Colgate University President Brian Casey, Obama said: "I cannot even imagine some of the things that are happening now."

He continued: "I try to think, what if I had said, 'You know what, Fox News, get out!' What would the consequences have been? It's unimaginable." The remark drew laughter from Casey and loud applause from the audience. (See clip below)

Hours before Obama's comments, Trump announced on Truth Social that he was barring these media outlets from the White House complex, citing their coverage of what he called "fake news".

Trump's decision triggered united condemnation from the press, with First Amendment and legal experts noting that the ban is unconstitutional.

The affected media outlets subsequently announced they were suing the Trump administration, with the complaint alleging that the President's decision was "as blatant an attack on the First Amendment as any we have ever seen, and as brazen a violation of our most basic constitutional principles".

Multiple TV networks were reportedly also planning to join in boycotting the daily White House press arrangement in solidarity with the affected outlets.

The Treasury Department under Obama had in 2009 at one point excluded Fox News — whose views Obama had once described as "destructive" — from a series of interviews with then-"pay czar" Kenneth Feinberg that were given to other major TV networks.

But his administration quickly reversed the decision, blaming the episode on a communication failure. At the time, the Washington bureau chiefs of the other major TV networks made clear that they would not participate in interviews if Fox News was excluded, and the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press also flagged the matter.

In his remarks at Colgate University, Obama turned the spotlight to "a group of people" in the United States (whom he estimated to make up roughly "30 to 35 percent" of Americans), saying they were untroubled by Trump's ban.

He said: "This means we have not built up an understanding of what democratic institutions require, and we have to rebuild that understanding."

He added: "I don't think it's inevitable, and I don't think it's too late in that regard, but we have to roll up our sleeves and get to work."
